title: Master Class | Philidor / Endgame Analysis | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: White tries the bishop to c4 against the Caro-Kann — the hillbilly bishop. It makes little sense here.
Because we hit it with d5, gaining a tempo on the bishop while striking the center.
teaches: d5 hits the c4 bishop with tempo

moves.spoken: On the check we block with the bishop to d7 rather than a knight — a small point of principle: don't move one piece repeatedly and trade it for a piece that's only moved once.
teaches: don’t trade a busy piece for a fresh one

moves.spoken: Don't fear the knight that lands on b5 — a lone piece on your side of the board is harmless, and you can even gain tempi hitting it later. We just develop.
teaches: a single intruding piece is not a threat

moves.spoken: So we develop the knight to c6 as if nothing is going on — because nothing is.
Once White plays c3 the a6 push becomes timely: the knight has lost its retreat, so if it jumps to d4 we take, saddling White with isolated, doubled center pawns — a real positional concession.
teaches: a6 to trap the knight into a bad structure

moves.spoken: After the trade White is left with an isolated pawn on d4 — that pawn becomes our target for the rest of the game.
teaches: the isolated d-pawn as a fixed target

moves.spoken: The bishop to d6 is an excellent square, eyeing the kingside and supporting our own play.
The knight goes to e7, not f6 — from e7 it can reroute to f5 or c6 to pile onto the d4-pawn.
teaches: Ne7 to reach the attacking squares

moves.spoken: With everything ready the plan is to stack pressure on the isolated pawn — a knight and the queen from b6.
The queen to b6 has a bonus: besides hitting d4, it discourages White's dark-squared bishop from developing. That extra benefit is why we move the queen before the knight.
teaches: choose the move order by the extra benefit

moves.spoken: The knight swings into f5 — active, and leaning hard on d4.
Rather than cash in on the pawn right away, we open the queenside with a5, prying open files to expose more weaknesses — flexibility over grabbing material too soon.
teaches: open a second front instead of rushing to win a pawn

moves.spoken: Now is the moment to take on d4 — we've made a fresh weakness on the queenside, so capturing opens a second front White can't defend everywhere at once.
teaches: time the capture to overload the defense

moves.spoken: After trading down, the queen is centralized and we're up two pawns with a passer. The winning method is textbook endgame technique: put the rook behind the passed pawn, bring the king in, and use the extra pawn as a decoy — sacrifice it to drag White's king offside and transition into a won pawn ending where our king marches into his position. Waiting moves and zugzwang do the rest.
teaches: the decoy-pawn transition to a won pawn ending

moves.spoken: Why we didn't just push e5 earlier: controlling the center isn't a race. You control it with pawns AND pieces, and pawns pushed out without piece support become targets — the whole hypermodern idea is to let the opponent over-extend and then pick the pawns off.
teaches: center control needs pieces, not just pawns
